title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
In 1939, surveyors hired by the federal Home Owners’ Loan Corporation graded every neighborhood in Detroit on a four-point scale. Grade A — colored green — meant “best”: new housing stock, “American business and professional men.” Grade D — colored red, the origin of the term redlining — meant “hazardous”: older housing, high Black population, and therefore a poor risk for a federally-backed mortgage (Mitchell & Franco, 2018).
Those grades shaped who could buy a home, build equity, and accumulate wealth over three generations (Aaronson, Hartley & Mazumder, 2021). Grade-D neighborhoods were starved of investment; grade-A suburbs — Grosse Pointe, Birmingham, Royal Oak — were built up with federal dollars, highway access, and restrictive deeds (Rothstein, 2017). When the auto industry contracted after 1970, the pain concentrated where it always had: in the city’s D-grade east and near-east side.
Today Detroit has two bus systems that don’t fully talk to each other. DDOT serves the city; SMART serves the suburbs. For decades there was no unified fare, no seamless transfer. The informal boundary between them traces, with uncomfortable precision, the boundary between the HOLC’s C/D zones and the A/B suburbs to the north.
What follows uses 2022 ACS 5-year estimates to ask whether the 1939 map still predicts who has a car, who takes the bus, and who can afford not to think about either. These are correlations, not causes. But the correlations are worth looking at.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
1. Where the lines were drawn
The Mapping Inequality project at the University of Richmond digitized the original HOLC appraisal maps from the National Archives (Nelson et al., 2023). Each polygon below is a neighborhood assessed by a local real estate agent under federal direction in 1939. The tooltips include the original neighborhood name.


Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook


Grade D polygons blanket the near east side, the lower east side, and much of the inner city — the areas home to the bulk of Detroit’s Black population, who had migrated north during and after World War I seeking industrial work. Grade A and B areas extend to the northwest and along the northern edge of the city, toward what would become the white-flight corridor into Oakland County.
What strikes you looking at the map is how geometric the logic was. The 8 Mile Road boundary and the Grosse Pointe city limits weren’t just municipal lines — they were where the grades changed, and where federal mortgage credit started and stopped.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
2. Car access by HOLC grade
In a metro region where transit is fragmented and job sprawl is severe, car access is not a lifestyle preference. A household without a car in the Detroit metro has limited access to the suburban job centers that now hold most of the region’s employment. The question is whether the historical grade still predicts who has a car today.









The gradient runs in the expected direction: grade-D tracts have the highest median share of car-free households, grade-A the lowest. But the spread within each grade is wide, particularly in grade D. That internal variation may reflect pockets of gentrification, areas with unusually good transit coverage, or the coarseness of assigning a single 1939 grade to a 2022 census tract.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
3. Who rides the bus
High transit use in a car-dependent region can mean two different things: genuine preference, or constrained necessity. The ACS tells us what people do, not why. Still, if transit commuting is concentrated in historically redlined tracts, it raises a question about whether the infrastructure serving those tracts is commensurate with the demand.









Transit use does climb from A to D, but that gradient exists within a region where the overall transit commute share is low — Detroit is still, structurally, a car city. The deeper question: are the bus routes serving grade-D tracts frequent enough and geographically comprehensive enough to reach suburban employment centers? DDOT and SMART have historically operated as separate systems with limited cross-boundary service (SEMCOG), a structural feature that the commute-share data surfaces but cannot explain.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
4. The economic gradient
The HOLC grades were, explicitly, an economic instrument — they determined access to federally-backed mortgage credit, the primary mechanism for building household wealth in postwar America. Eighty years later, the income and poverty gradient across the same geography is still legible.









The income gradient is steep and consistent. This is not surprising — it’s roughly what the redlining literature has documented nationally (Aaronson, Hartley & Mazumder, 2021). But the Detroit case has particular features: the collapse of the auto industry accelerated decline in areas that were already disinvested, and racial exclusion from the suburbs was enforced not just by HOLC grades but by deed covenants, blockbusting, and the deliberate routing of I-75 and I-94 through Black neighborhoods in the 1950s and 60s (Rothstein, 2017).
The gradient is real. The mechanism is overdetermined. HOLC grades may be one thread among several, not the whole story.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
5. The geography of car access
The box plots above summarize distributions by grade, but the spatial pattern matters on its own. Where exactly are the car-free households, and do they cluster in ways that overlap the 1939 boundary lines?


Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook


The darkest areas — highest car-free rates — cluster in the inner city, overlapping the red-outlined grade-D polygons. The gradient is not perfectly clean: some grade-C tracts show high car-free rates, and suburban grade-A areas have near-zero rates. But the spatial coincidence is striking enough to motivate the next chart.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
text:
6. The compounding trap
Low income limits car access. Low car access limits job access. Job access limits income. The scatter below asks whether this trap clusters in the areas that the HOLC graded as hazardous.









Grade-D points cluster toward the upper-left quadrant: low income, high car-free rate. Grade-A points cluster lower-right. The clustering is not absolute — there is overlap between grades, and some grade-D tracts have incomes and car-access rates closer to the metro median, likely reflecting ongoing neighborhood change. But the center of gravity of each grade is where you would expect it if the 1939 map were still doing work.
This is a cross-sectional snapshot. It cannot tell us whether redlining caused this clustering, or whether the same underlying forces that shaped the 1939 grades are still at work through other mechanisms.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
section: 8. Bus stop access across HOLC grades
text:
8. Bus stop access across HOLC grades
The transit commute share in §3 reflects revealed behavior — who actually rides. But it cannot tell us whether the infrastructure is there to use. Two more basic questions: Is there a bus stop within a 5-minute walk of a typical resident in each grade zone? And if so, how often does that bus actually come?
We use OpenStreetMap stop locations queried via the Overpass API — covering both DDOT and SMART — for the proximity question, and SMART GTFS schedule data for frequency. DDOT’s GTFS feed is not publicly accessible, so the frequency picture is partial: SMART primarily serves the suburbs, meaning grades A and B have better frequency coverage in this data. That bias is worth keeping in mind.





























Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook


The bus-stop geography inverts the intuition you might carry from the economic and car-access charts. Because Detroit’s inner city is the densest part of the metro, it actually has relatively high stop density — grade-D tracts are often within a short walk of a DDOT stop. The suburban grade-A and grade-B zones, built around the automobile, have sparser stop networks and longer walk distances.
But proximity alone is not service. The SMART GTFS data shows that in the outer-ring zones — where stops do exist — they come infrequently. The compounding problem for grade-D residents runs in the opposite direction: stops are nearby, but the ACS commute data suggests transit use remains constrained even where stops are present. The most likely explanation is not stop proximity but network reach: a dense stop network that loops within a neighborhood is not the same as one that connects reliably to suburban employment centers.
The most important missing piece is a job-accessibility isochrone — how many jobs can a resident reach by transit within 45 minutes? That would require GTFS from both agencies and an origin-destination travel-time matrix. The LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES) provide the employment side of this equation; the transit side remains unavailable in a public, consolidated format for this region.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
section: 7. What the data can’t tell us
text:
7. What the data can’t tell us
On transit adequacy. The ACS tells us who takes transit; it doesn’t tell us whether transit goes where people need it to go. The bus stop analysis in §8 is a first pass. What’s still missing: what share of grade-D tract residents are within walking distance of a route with 30-minute or better headways? That would require GTFS from both agencies layered onto this spatial analysis.
On job accessibility. Car-free rate is only a problem if the jobs reachable without a car are insufficient. A follow-on analysis using LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES) could calculate the number of jobs reachable within 45 minutes by transit for each tract — a much sharper mobility indicator than commute mode share.
On displacement and change. These are 2022 tracts on a 1939 map. Corktown — historically grade C/D, adjacent to the Ford-backed Michigan Central Station development — is changing rapidly. The snapshot doesn’t capture whether the residents who benefit from infrastructure investment are the same people who bore the costs of disinvestment.
On causation. The correlations here are consistent with HOLC grades having long-run effects on neighborhood outcomes (Aaronson, Hartley & Mazumder, 2021). They are also consistent with explanations that have little to do with the HOLC maps themselves: racial exclusion enforced through private deed covenants, federal highway routing that severed Black neighborhoods from job centers, blockbusting by real estate agents (Rothstein, 2017). Disentangling these mechanisms would require something like a regression discontinuity design — comparing tracts on either side of a grade boundary that were otherwise similar in 1939.

title: Redlining’s long shadow: mobility and opportunity in greater Detroit
section: A note on method and data
text:
A note on method and data
The grade assigned to each census tract reflects whichever HOLC grade covered the largest share of the tract’s area within HOLC-surveyed territory, provided that share was at least 60%. Tracts where no single grade dominated are excluded from the grade-stratified charts but retained in the maps. The 60% threshold is a judgment call; at 50% or 70% the counts change but the directional pattern does not.
ACS 5-year 2022 estimates smooth year-to-year noise but can mask rapid recent change. Tract-level averages obscure within-tract variation, which can be substantial in larger or heterogeneous tracts. Census tract boundaries were retrieved via pygris. Bus stop locations are from OpenStreetMap (queried Overpass API, March 2026) and cover stops tagged as highway=bus_stop or public_transport=stop_position within the three-county metro area. Transit frequency reflects SMART GTFS only; DDOT GTFS is not publicly available.
The gradient documented here is real. The mechanism is a question — one that the data motivates but does not resolve.

Data sources

HOLC neighborhood boundaries: Mapping Inequality, Digital Scholarship Lab, University of Richmond.
ACS 5-year 2022 estimates: U.S. Census Bureau.
Census tract boundaries: pygris (TIGER/Line 2022).
Bus stop locations: OpenStreetMap contributors via Overpass API.
Transit schedules: SMART GTFS (retrieved March 2026).

References

Aaronson, D., Hartley, D., & Mazumder, B. (2021). The effects of the 1930s HOLC ‘redlining’ maps on CD outcomes. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 13(4), 355–392. doi:10.1257/pol.20190414
Mitchell, B., & Franco, J. (2018). HOLC ‘Redlining’ Maps: The persistent structure of segregation and economic inequality. NCRC. ncrc.org/holc
Nelson, R. K., Winling, L., Marciano, R., & Connolly, N. (2023). Mapping Inequality: Redlining in New Deal America. American Panorama, University of Richmond. dsl.richmond.edu/panorama/redlining
Rothstein, R. (2017). The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America. Liveright/Norton. wwnorton.com

title: American national park visits: location density and visitation rates
text:
This project investigates whether the spatial distribution of U.S. national parks influences how often they are visited. The central question is intuitive but surprisingly under-examined: do parks that sit near other parks benefit from that proximity?
For this project, our claim is that American National Parks visitation rates are higher in regions where national parks are geographically closer together, suggesting travelers are more likely to visit multiple parks within a dense cluster.
Three guiding questions structure the analysis:
This hypothesis is based on the intuitive assumption that geographic proximity facilitates multi-park trips, potentially through reduced travel costs, shared infrastructure, and the ability to visit multiple destinations in a single vacation. If correct, we would expect tightly clustered parks to show higher per-park visitation rates than regions with widely dispersed parks.

title: American national park visits: location density and visitation rates
text:
Data choices and justifications
Our first significant data choice was calculating the distances between the parks in each region. As the class dataset did not include geographical data, we decided to import an external dataset and matched parks by name to merge the data. After some light data cleaning to remove duplicates and standardize park names, we utilized the latitude and longitude in the Haversine Formula to calculate the distance between all pairs of parks across regions. We chose to use this formula due to its ability to calculate distances across a sphere using these coordinates accurately, as mentioned in the educational data science site GeeksForGeeks.
Additionally, after finding the Haversine distance between each park, we used a multiplier of 1.4 on each value to account for the variations in road structures (as the distances between each park are likely not straight lines). According to a study published in the National Library of Medicine titled “A Nationwide Comparison of Driving Distance Versus Straight-Line Distance to Hospitals”, in nearly “all locations within the United States,” applying a detour index of about 1.4 to the “straight-line distance” is an “adequate proxy for travel distance”. Though this does not account for more severe detours or uncrossable geographic features (roadblocks, lakes, rivers, etc.), we thought it was a good first step to take to approximate the distance (in miles).
Finally, among our three approaches (discussed below in more detail), one approach involved investigating whether parks closer to metropolitan areas showed any changes in visitation compared to more remote areas. To do this, we used the US Metro Areas Database, which contains coordinates and population data. Then, for each metro area, we used the same Haversine distance calculation to calculate its distance between all parks, only keeping the parks that were within a 300-mile radius of a metro area to ensure we only examined parks that were reasonably accessible from major metropolitan cities (and minimizing any potential bias, such as parks with very low visits or that were remote).

title: American national park visits: location density and visitation rates
text:
Approaches
We used three complementary spatial approaches to test our hypothesis at different scales.

Approach 1: neighbor count
For this approach, we used a pairwise distance calculation, combined with a Pearson Correlation (r) analysis, to test the relationship between park clustering and visitation at an individual park level. For neighbor counting, we defined a spatial radius of 300 miles, which is roughly a 4–6 hour drive. For each park, we counted the number of other parks within this radius and grouped the parks into categories: Isolated (0), Few (1–2), Some (3–5), and Many (6+) neighbors. In addition to calculating the correlation (r) based on the neighbor count (independent variable) and the total recreation visits for each park (dependent variable), we explored the visitation distributions across these categories through summary statistics and box plots.


Approach 2: grid-based analysis
For this approach, we used geographical binning (as well as per-park normalization and correlation analysis to minimize any effects regional distribution may have had) to test clustering effects at a tighter spatial scale. To do this, we divided the U.S. into a grid (we chose 150 by 150 miles, roughly) and converted the grid size from miles to degrees, approximated using 1 degree ≈ 69 miles for both latitude and longitude. While this created some distortion at higher latitudes, most parks fell within similar latitude bands, minimizing the effect.
For each grid square, we calculated park count, total visits, and average visit per park (total visits divided by park count). Without this normalization, grids with more parks would automatically have higher total visits. By averaging visits per park, the analysis isolates the effect of density rather than just quantity.
To have meaningful clustering comparisons, we also only counted the grids that contained at least two parks. We calculated r based on the number of parks in each grid (our independent variable) and the average visits per park in that grid (dependent variable).


Approach 3: metro areas
For each metropolitan area, we identified all parks within a radius and calculated park count near that metro, total visits from all nearby parks, and average visits per park. This normalization was, again, essential, as metros surrounded by many parks should not automatically appear as more “successful” simply because they had more parks within their radius. By normalizing to average visits per park, we were able to test whether individual parks near clustered metro areas receive more visits than parks near metro areas with fewer park options, potentially due to shared tourism infrastructure or marketing.
This approach also allowed us to examine whether metro population size correlates with park visitation, helping distinguish between clustering effects and general urban accessibility effects.

Neighbor count analysis
Our neighbor count analysis had a correlation coefficient of r = 0.020, indicating that there is virtually no correlation between the number of neighbors a park has and its visitation at the 300-mile scale.
Our hypothesis is not supported at the individual park level. For example, Acadia Park, which is completely isolated, received 4.5 times more visits than Capitol Reef, which had 8 neighbors (the highest neighbor count). Capitol Reef, besides being the most clustered park, had 30M visits, and Bryce Canyon was right behind (7 neighbors, 54M visits). Despite having zero neighbors (within the 300-mile radius), Acadia still received 134M visits. This is perhaps the clearest example that proximity to other parks does not predict higher visitation.

Grid-based analysis
For our grid-based approach, we found a strong, positive correlation between park proximity and the number of visits. From the 54 grids we created, only seven grids had more than two parks — five grids had two parks, and two grids had three parks. The correlation coefficient of r = 0.934, though extremely strong, only occurred because we controlled for regional differences (through creating grids). After creating our grids, we saw high-density clusters (e.g. Bryce/Grand Canyon/Zion Parks, with an average of 120M visits per park; Kings Canyon/Sequoia/Yosemite Parks, with an average of 77M visits) as well as grids with lower density (e.g. Carlsbad/Guadalupe Parks with an average of 16M). This suggests the visitation benefits of clustering, in our grid analysis, only occur at tighter spatial scales. When we increase the threshold from 150 to 300 miles, for example, we get 14 grid squares with more than two parks and one grid square with five parks. The correlation then becomes −0.105, suggesting that at an even slightly broader threshold, the clustering “benefits” for visitations disappear. Once parks are more spaced out, other influencing factors, such as accessibility or regional tourism, take precedence over clustering.

Metro areas
Our metro area analysis found that there was a slightly negative correlation between the number of parks in a metropolitan area and both average visits and average visits per park (−0.113 and −0.018, respectively). There were 282 metro areas with national parks within 300 miles of it. The parks that were closer to metro areas appeared to have fewer visits per park, rather than more. While a park’s proximity to urban areas doesn’t directly enhance clustering benefits, this may indicate that the parks have competition for visits (e.g. parks closer to metro areas may have to compete with restaurants, museums, and other entertainment options for visits). In other words, park proximity alone is not a sufficient driver for increased visitation.

title: American national park visits: location density and visitation rates
text:
Conclusion
Our hypothesis that geographic clustering increases park visitation is context-dependent. At the broad spatial scale (300-mile radius), clustering shows no effect (r = 0.020), suggesting individual park characteristics dominate visitation decisions. However, within tight geographic clusters (150-mile grids), we DO observe a very strong positive relationship (r = 0.934), indicating that when parks are “truly” close, multi-park tourism does boost visitation. This suggests a distance threshold: parks must be within day-trip distance (~150 miles) for clustering benefits to materialize.

title: American national park visits: location density and visitation rates
text:
Viability of claim
Due to our choices of aggregating park visitations and normalizing across regions in our grid-based analysis, we cannot easily generalize our claim. Particularly with our aggregation — because we focus on total park visits, rather than investigating visitation types or seasonal patterns, our ability to conclude why specific parks receive a certain level of visitors is limited. Our inclusion of a distance threshold also means our findings are mainly applicable to densely clustered parks, rather than those spread out over larger areas. However, we can still evaluate the broader structural relationship between average visitation numbers and the distribution of parks within regions.
Despite these limitations, we do believe the main pattern in our claim would hold in the future. The general trend identified that tightly clustered parks (specifically, within 150 miles of one another) would see higher average visits and would likely remain the same. The number of visits to parks in a region will not solely depend on their proximity to one another; other factors (such as accessibility, tourism, marketing, isolated regions, or climate) will remain factors. The geographic structure of the park regions and surrounding population density will stay stable over time.
If this claim were to hold for other types of parks, it would likely depend on whether the other park systems had a similar geographic clustering and the feasibility of traveling. For example, in other parks that were laid out in a similar way to the national parks (e.g., regions with many parks in proximity that could be realistically visited in a single trip), using proximity to investigate visitation rates will likely be fruitful. For park systems with fewer parks or that are more geographically isolated, proximity is unlikely to correlate to an increase in visitation rates on its own. Future work to ensure our claim is more broadly applicable (as mentioned above) would include integrating temporal analysis and visitation type.

title: Exploring U.S. Airfare Trends
text:
Nominal vs. inflation-adjusted airfare, 1995–2025










Findings
The dual-line chart above shows the central tension of modern air travel that we’re examining: the perceived cost versus the real, inflation-adjusted value. While the Current Dollar (Nominal) Fare (the red line) shows a general upward trend (often giving travelers the impression that flights are constantly getting more expensive), the Inflation-Adjusted Fare (the green line) tells a different story: Despite episodic spikes, the real cost of flying has declined significantly over the past three decades. Using Q1 1995 as a benchmark, the long-term trend shows a major decrease in what an airfare ticket costs relative to other consumer goods. This shows the impact of deregulation and increasing competition from low-cost carriers.
The chart also illustrates how major external shocks interrupt the long-term decline. We examined:

9/11 Attacks (2001): The initial drop in demand caused fares to plunge.
2008 Oil Crisis: This caused the most acute spike outside of the pandemic. As fuel costs hit record highs, the inflation-adjusted fare surged, forcing airlines to pass the expense directly to consumers.
COVID-19 Pandemic (2020): Fares cratered to a historic low, demonstrating that even rock-bottom prices couldn’t entice travelers during the global shutdown.

The overall takeaway for the traveler is that the cost of flying is not steadily increasing; it is an economic roller coaster where long-term affordability is periodically interrupted by massive, yet brief, external shocks.


Airfare over time with year filter










Average airfare by city, 1995
Highlight individual cities to compare fares.









Quarter-over-quarter airfare change during COVID-19, 2018–2022
Measuring and visualizing quarter-over-quarter percentage changes to highlight the magnitude and volatility of price shocks during the pandemic period.










Findings
The most interesting feature of the chart is the deep-red bar corresponding to the second quarter of 2020 (Q2 2020). This bar represents the largest quarterly decline in average domestic airfare in the dataset’s history. The average domestic airfare dropped by approximately 19.8% in Q2 2020 compared to Q1 2020. This is the quarter when most travel restrictions were enacted. Following the massive negative spike, the chart shows a pattern of extreme volatility, characterized by alternating large green (positive) and red (negative) bars in 2021 and 2022. This is possibly due to the market’s erratic attempts to find a new equilibrium as demand pulsed back and forth. The bars representing the years 2018 and 2019 are relatively small and centered around the zero line, demonstrating the pre-pandemic stability of the market. The dramatic scale of the 2020 drop and subsequent rebound starkly highlights the event as an unprecedented external shock to the airline economy.











Airfare and jet fuel prices, 1995–present








This visualization shows how closely domestic airfares have tracked jet fuel prices over the past 30 years—and where that relationship has broken down. In the early years of the series, when fuel was cheap and relatively stable, airfares clustered tightly as well, reflecting a period of intense airline competition and steady consumer demand. The path then swings sharply to the right in the mid-2000s, during the global oil shock, when jet fuel prices surged far faster than ticket prices—evidence that airlines absorbed much of the hit through fees, capacity cuts, and operational changes rather than passing the full cost to travelers. The steep downward drop marks the COVID-19 collapse, when both fuel costs and fares plunged simultaneously to record lows. And on the far right edge, the line bends upward again during the 2022–23 rebound, as high fuel prices and a surge in post-pandemic travel pushed fares to their highest levels in years. Taken together, the chart reveals a long-term dance between fuel costs and ticket prices, punctuated by economic shocks that pull the two series apart before they fall back into step.
